title: Mortgage Operations Posting Standard for Payments on Home Mortgage Loans
content:
Mortgage Operations posts payments received on Home Mortgage Loans notes on the basis set out here.

## Which loans a payment posts to

A payment posts only to a loan whose status is active, delinquent or forbearance. The status is read from the bank's record of that loan, correlated to the loan the payment is made against, before the payment is posted.

## A payment smaller than one full installment

A payment smaller than one full installment is handled on the program's basis for a partial payment and is returned to the borrower without being applied.

## The order in which a payment is applied

Each full installment within the payment is applied to interest, then to principal, then to escrow. Any amount beyond whole installments is applied to fees due, and then, when it is at least the program's smallest extra principal payment accepted, to principal as an extra principal payment.

Late charges are never deducted from an installment, so a timely full installment is never made late by an unpaid late charge.

No penalty applies to principal prepaid.

## Payment from a Piedmont Crescent Bank checking account

A payment made from a Piedmont Crescent Bank checking account debits that account.

## Worked figures on hypothetical inputs

Take a loan on a program whose smallest extra principal payment accepted is $25.00, whose principal and interest payment is $1500.00 and whose monthly escrow deposit is $300.00, so that one full installment is $1800.00.

- A payment of $1750.00 is smaller than one full installment. It is returned to the borrower and none of it is applied.
- A payment of $1900.00 carries one whole installment of $1800.00, which is applied to interest, then principal, then escrow. The remaining $100.00 is applied to fees due. If $40.00 of fees were due, $60.00 is left; being at least $25.00, it goes to principal as an extra principal payment.
- A payment of $3600.00 carries two whole installments, each applied to interest, then principal, then escrow, with nothing beyond them.
